also.hook: Turing supplied both of AI's founding documents: the 1936 paper proving one universal machine could compute anything computable, and the 1950 paper asking whether machines can think. The first made computers possible; the second made artificial intelligence a research question rather than a fantasy.
also.name: Alan Turing
also.moniker: Father of Theoretical Computer Science and AI

also.hook: Alec Radford studied at the Franklin W. Olin College of Engineering before working on early deep learning projects, including the 2015 DCGAN paper that became a widely used template for stable generative adversarial network training. He joined OpenAI as one of its early research scientists and went on to lead or co-author a string of the field's most consequential papers: GPT-1 and GPT-2, which established generative pretraining as a path to general-purpose language models, GPT-3, CLIP, which paired vision and language in a single contrastively trained model, and Whisper, an open multilingual speech recognition system. Despite being one of the most cited researchers behind modern large language models, Radford keeps a low public profile and rarely gives interviews, letting the papers speak for the work.
also.name: Alec Radford
also.moniker: Research Scientist, OpenAI

also.hook: Zhavoronkov built Insilico Medicine to prove that generative AI could do more than analyze biology, it could design new drug candidates outright, and Rentosertib, discovered and designed by Insilico's AI pipeline, became one of the first such molecules to reach human clinical trials.
also.name: Alex Zhavoronkov
also.moniker: Pioneer of AI-Driven Drug Discovery

also.hook: Ng did more than any single figure to turn machine learning from a graduate-school subject into a skill anyone could learn online, while simultaneously building the industrial-scale infrastructure, Google Brain among it, that made deep learning practical at big-tech scale.
also.name: Andrew Ng
also.moniker: AI Educator and Deep Learning Pioneer

also.hook: Rabinovich arrived at the Longuet-Higgins Prize, the computer vision field's highest honor for work that has stood the test of time, the same year his startup was acquired and he became CTO of a public company. His arc from Google research to Magic Leap's human-centered AR, to founding an AI meeting tool, to leading AI at one of the world's largest freelance platforms is a compressed version of the field's own evolution: from perception research to multimodal generation to enterprise deployment.
also.name: Andrew Rabinovich
also.moniker: CTO and Head of AI at Upwork

also.hook: Arthur Mensch spent two and a half years researching large language models at Google DeepMind before deciding, alongside longtime friends Guillaume Lample and Timothee Lacroix, that a European lab could compete at the frontier while keeping its models open. The three co-founded Mistral AI in Paris in April 2023, and Mensch has run the company as CEO since, positioning it as an open-weight counterweight to closed labs in the US. He holds a doctorate in machine learning from Paris-Saclay University, following earlier study at Ecole Polytechnique and Telecom Paris, and in 2025 was named a Knight of the French National Order of Merit.
also.name: Arthur Mensch
also.moniker: Co-Founder and CEO, Mistral AI

also.hook: Barret Zoph began his research career at the University of Southern California's Information Sciences Institute working on machine translation before joining Google Brain as a staff research scientist. There he co-authored Neural Architecture Search with Reinforcement Learning, one of the founding papers of the field that automated the design of neural network architectures, and later worked on sparse and mixture-of-experts techniques for scaling language models efficiently. He moved to OpenAI, rising to Vice President of Research for Post-Training, where his team worked on alignment, tool use, evaluations, and the multimodal capabilities behind ChatGPT and the OpenAI API. In 2025 he left to co-found Thinking Machines Lab alongside Mira Murati, becoming the company's Chief Technology Officer and helping build an AI research and product company focused on making AI systems more customizable and generally capable.
also.name: Barret Zoph
also.moniker: Co-founder and CTO, Thinking Machines Lab

also.hook: Sengupta has built enterprise AI functions from scratch at four different organizations, AXA XL, Zebra Technologies, and now JPMorgan Chase, while maintaining an active academic research career that produced over 9,100 citations and a co-authored analysis of the EU AI Act, a rare combination of frontier research credentials and boardroom-level AI deployment experience.
also.name: Biswa Sengupta
also.moniker: Chief AI Technologist and Architect of JPMorgan's LLM Suite

also.hook: Colin Raffel studied at Columbia University, where his early research focused on music information retrieval, before joining Google Brain as a research scientist. There he led the team that published Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer, introducing the T5 model and its text-to-text framing of natural language processing tasks, later published in the Journal of Machine Learning Research. He subsequently moved into academia, and today he is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at the University of Toronto, an Associate Research Director at the Vector Institute, and a Faculty Researcher at Hugging Face. His current research group focuses on decentralizing, democratizing, and de-risking large-scale AI, including work on collaborative and communication-efficient training methods.
also.name: Colin Raffel
also.moniker: Associate Professor, University of Toronto and Vector Institute

also.hook: Nguyen holds a Stanford PhD combining AI with bioengineering and spent years on deepfake detection at Facebook AI and Adobe before research internships in Fei-Fei Li's and Leonidas Guibas's labs and at Google DeepMind's co-scientist team. He now leads Radical Numerics, a company he co-founded to build what he describes as general biological intelligence.
also.name: Eric Nguyen
also.moniker: Co-Founder and CEO, Radical Numerics

also.hook: Guillaume Lample spent his early career at Facebook AI Research pushing multilingual natural language processing forward, then helped build the LLaMA models that reshaped the open-weight AI race. In April 2023 he left Meta to co-found Mistral AI with Arthur Mensch and Timothee Lacroix, taking the role of Chief Scientist. Within two months the young company had raised a European-record seed round, and within six months it had shipped an open-weight model that rivals judged competitive with far larger closed systems. He remains the technical architect behind Mistral's model line, from the first 7B release through its largest frontier models.
also.name: Guillaume Lample
also.moniker: Co-founder and Chief Scientist, Mistral AI

also.hook: Hugo Touvron holds two bachelor's degrees, from Ecole Polytechnique and Paris Dauphine University, and three master's degrees in mathematics and computer science from Ecole Polytechnique, ENS Paris-Saclay, and ENSTA ParisTech. He joined Facebook AI Research in November 2019 as a resident PhD student advised by Herve Jegou at Facebook and Matthieu Cord at Sorbonne University, where his early work centered on data-efficient image transformers and vision transfer learning, including the DeiT and DeiT III papers. He then moved into large language models, becoming lead author of LLaMA, Meta's open-weights foundation language model released in February 2023, followed by Llama 2 in July 2023 and a contribution to Code Llama in August 2023. His work helped establish the open-weights LLaMA family as a widely used alternative to closed frontier models.
also.name: Hugo Touvron
also.moniker: Research Scientist, Meta AI (FAIR)

also.hook: Jared Kaplan built his early career as a theoretical physicist, holding a PhD from Harvard and a faculty position at Johns Hopkins studying quantum gravity and conformal field theory. Starting in 2018 he turned that background toward machine learning, working on how language model performance scales with compute, data and parameters, research his own university describes as feeding into GPT-3. In 2021 he co-founded Anthropic and became its Chief Science Officer, leading the technical research behind models like Claude and methods such as Constitutional AI. He still holds his Johns Hopkins physics appointment alongside his role at Anthropic.
also.name: Jared Kaplan
also.moniker: Co-founder and Chief Science Officer, Anthropic

also.hook: Jonathan Ross started what became Google's Tensor Processing Unit as an internal side project, then left to found Groq in 2016, building a chip architecture designed purely for AI inference. Groq's language processing units made the company one of the most closely watched hardware challengers to Nvidia. In December 2025 Nvidia took a non-exclusive license to Groq's technology and hired Ross along with most of Groq's engineering team, a deal that returned billions of dollars to Groq's shareholders and moved its founder inside the company his chips were built to compete with. Ross now works at Nvidia as its chief software architect, and has spoken candidly about the leadership mistakes he made running Groq for nearly a decade.
also.name: Jonathan Ross
also.moniker: Chief Software Architect at Nvidia, founder of Groq

also.hook: Reis-Filho built his career deciphering cancer genomics at the bench, at the Institute of Cancer Research and then as Chief of Experimental Pathology at Memorial Sloan Kettering, before moving to AstraZeneca to apply AI foundation models and agentic frameworks directly to drug discovery and clinical development, one of the clearer examples of a working oncologist becoming an enterprise AI leader.
also.name: Jorge Reis-Filho
also.moniker: Chief of AI for Science Innovation at AstraZeneca

also.hook: Margaret Mitchell is an AI researcher whose work focuses on documentation and transparency practices meant to make machine learning systems more accountable. Working across natural language processing and computer vision, she has held research roles at Microsoft Research, Google, and now Hugging Face. In 2018 she was the lead author of Model Cards for Model Reporting, a paper written with a team of Google and academic researchers, including Timnit Gebru, that proposed short standardized documents to accompany released machine learning models describing how they perform across different conditions and demographic groups. The model card format she helped design was later adopted widely across the AI industry. At Hugging Face she works on the company's Society and Ethics research efforts and contributes to open research initiatives such as the BigScience and BigCode workshops. Her research continues to center on practical tools, such as model documentation and bias evaluation methods, that let developers and the public better understand what a given AI system does and does not do well.
also.name: Margaret Mitchell
also.moniker: AI ethics researcher and co-creator of Model Cards

also.hook: Mark Chen has been at OpenAI since 2018, moving from quantitative trading into leading some of the company's most visible research programs. He co-led the team that built DALL-E, directed the vision work that gave GPT-4 its multimodal capabilities, and oversaw Codex, the model behind GitHub Copilot. In March 2025 OpenAI named him Chief Research Officer, a role focused on integrating research and product development so new capabilities move into deployment faster. He also coaches the USA Computing Olympiad team, a pastime that tracks with his own path through competitive mathematics and computer science at MIT.
also.name: Mark Chen
also.moniker: Chief Research Officer, OpenAI

also.hook: Norman Jouppi earned a master's degree in electrical engineering from Northwestern University in 1980 and a PhD in electrical engineering from Stanford University in 1984, where he was one of the principal architects of the MIPS microprocessor. He spent much of his early career at Digital Equipment Corporation's Western Research Laboratory researching computer memory systems, microprocessor architecture and graphics accelerators, work that carried through DEC's acquisition by Compaq and Compaq's later acquisition by Hewlett-Packard, where he was named an HP Senior Fellow in 2010. He joined Google in the early 2010s and became technical lead for the company's Tensor Processing Units from their inception, with the first generation deployed in Google datacenters starting in 2015. He was lead author of "In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit," published at ISCA in 2017, which documented the chip's real-world performance and became one of the most cited papers in computer architecture. He now holds the title of Vice President and Engineering Fellow at Google, continuing to lead AI infrastructure and TPU development.
also.name: Norman Jouppi
also.moniker: Chief architect of Google's Tensor Processing Unit

also.hook: Robin Rombach is the lead author of the Latent Diffusion Models paper produced with the CompVis group at LMU Munich, the research that became the technical basis for Stable Diffusion. After a physics degree at Heidelberg and a PhD at LMU Munich, he continued the work as Research Director at Stability AI before leaving in 2024. In August 2024 he co-founded Black Forest Labs with two of his Latent Diffusion co-authors, Patrick Esser and Andreas Blattmann, releasing the FLUX.1 image model on launch day. He now runs Black Forest Labs as CEO from labs in Freiburg and San Francisco, and in 2026 spoke at the G7 alongside heads of state to argue for keeping frontier visual AI development open.
also.name: Robin Rombach
also.moniker: Co-founder and CEO, Black Forest Labs

also.hook: Tim Dettmers built his career on the wager that making large models run on far less hardware would open up who gets to do AI research at all. His PhD work at the University of Washington, advised by Luke Zettlemoyer, produced LLM.int8() in 2022 and then QLoRA in 2023, a method that let a 65 billion parameter language model be fine-tuned on a single 48 gigabyte GPU. He maintains bitsandbytes, the open-source quantization library those methods run on, and in 2024 he became an Assistant Professor at Carnegie Mellon University while continuing as a Research Scientist at the Allen Institute for AI. His own faculty page describes his focus as making foundation models accessible to researchers and practitioners by reducing their resource requirements.
also.name: Tim Dettmers
also.moniker: Assistant Professor, Carnegie Mellon University

also.hook: Timothée Lacroix worked on Meta's LLaMA language models as a researcher at Facebook AI Research before leaving in 2023 to co-found Mistral AI with Arthur Mensch and Guillaume Lample. As Chief Technology Officer he leads the Paris-based company's research and technical direction, the work behind models like Mistral Large and the Le Chat assistant. Mistral positioned itself from the outset as a European counterweight to closed, US-based AI labs, releasing open-weight models such as Mistral 7B alongside its commercial offerings. Lacroix trained as a computer scientist at the Ecole Normale Superieure and holds a doctorate tied to the University of Paris-Est.
also.name: Timothée Lacroix
also.moniker: Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer, Mistral AI

also.hook: Tri Dao's PhD work at Stanford, co-advised by Christopher Re and Stefano Ermon, produced FlashAttention, a fast, memory-efficient attention algorithm that cut a Transformer's memory use from quadratic to linear in sequence length. Presented at NeurIPS in 2022 and later extended in FlashAttention-2 and FlashAttention-3, it became a piece of infrastructure that most large language models now train and run on. He joined Together AI as a co-founder and Chief Scientist around the time he finished his PhD, and is also an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Princeton University, where he leads the Dao AI Lab.
also.name: Tri Dao
also.moniker: Assistant Professor, Princeton University, and Chief Scientist, Together AI

profiles.hook: Aidan Gomez studied mathematics and computer science as an undergraduate at the University of Toronto, working with Roger Grosse, before interning as a student researcher at Google Brain. There, working alongside Jakob Uszkoreit and other Google Brain researchers, he was one of eight co-authors of the 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need, which introduced the Transformer architecture that replaced recurrence and convolution with self-attention and went on to underpin most later large language models. He also co-authored the Reversible Residual Network (RevNet) paper on memory-efficient deep network training. He then pursued doctoral studies in machine learning at the University of Oxford, advised by Yarin Gal and Yee Whye Teh, while leading a research team at the nonprofit lab FOR.ai. In 2019 he co-founded Cohere in Toronto, where as CEO he has helped the company raise close to a billion dollars across four funding rounds and build enterprise-focused large language models.

profiles.moniker: Co-founder and CEO, Cohere

profiles.hook: Albert Gu is one of the two authors of Mamba, the 2023 paper that showed a state space model could match Transformer-quality language modeling while scaling linearly instead of quadratically with sequence length. The work built on his earlier S4 research from his Stanford PhD under Chris Re, and it gave the field its first credible architectural alternative to attention. Gu now holds both an academic and a commercial base for that idea, teaching as an Assistant Professor in Carnegie Mellon's Machine Learning Department while serving as Chief Scientist and Co-Founder at Cartesia, a startup applying state space models to real-time voice and audio AI. TIME named him to its 100 Most Influential People in AI in 2024 for that combination of research and applied work.

profiles.hook: Aleksa Gordić studied electrical engineering with a focus on computer science and electronics, graduating in 2017. He worked as a machine learning engineer at Microsoft from 2018 to 2021 before joining Google DeepMind as a research engineer in 2021. In 2020 he started The AI Epiphany, a YouTube channel and blog that walks viewers through deep learning papers and code, and he published open source reimplementations of models such as Graph Attention Networks and the original Transformer. He left DeepMind in 2023 to focus on independent research and teaching, and led development of YugoGPT, an open large language model for Serbian and neighboring South Slavic languages. In 2025 he joined P-1 AI, a startup building AI systems for physical world engineering tasks.

profiles.hook: Alex Graves earned a degree in theoretical physics from the University of Edinburgh before completing a PhD in artificial intelligence at the Technical University of Munich, supervised by Jürgen Schmidhuber at the Dalle Molle Institute for Artificial Intelligence Research. During his doctoral work he introduced Connectionist Temporal Classification in 2006, a method that let recurrent neural networks train directly on unsegmented sequences such as speech and handwriting. In 2009 his CTC-trained LSTM networks became the first recurrent neural networks to win international handwriting recognition competitions. After postdoctoral work with Schmidhuber and with Geoffrey Hinton at the University of Toronto, he joined Google DeepMind in London as a research scientist, where he introduced the Neural Turing Machine and its successor, the Differentiable Neural Computer. In 2023 he published work on Bayesian Flow Networks and moved to InstaDeep as a Staff Research Scientist.

profiles.moniker: Pioneer of connectionist temporal classification and neural memory architectures

profiles.hook: Alex Krizhevsky was a graduate student in computer science at the University of Toronto, working under Geoffrey Hinton alongside fellow student Ilya Sutskever. In 2012 the three published ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks, describing a large convolutional network, later known as AlexNet, that used GPU training and a new regularization technique to sharply cut image classification error rates. A variant of the network won the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge that year by a wide margin, a result widely credited with convincing the broader field that deep neural networks, trained at scale on GPUs, could outperform earlier computer vision approaches. Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton founded DNNresearch Inc. to build on the work, and in March 2013 Google acquired the company, bringing Krizhevsky and Sutskever onto Google's research staff while Hinton divided his time between Google and the university.

profiles.moniker: Co-creator of AlexNet

profiles.hook: Alexey Kurakin built an early research career studying pattern recognition and hand gesture recognition before moving into deep learning. At Google he became one of the first researchers to show that adversarial examples, inputs deliberately perturbed to fool machine learning models, remain effective even after being printed and photographed with a camera, publishing this result with Ian Goodfellow and Samy Bengio as Adversarial Examples in the Physical World. The same period he co-authored Adversarial Machine Learning at Scale, studying how adversarial training could be applied to large image classifiers. In 2016 he demonstrated a physical adversarial attack live at the GeekPwn security conference alongside Ian Goodfellow. He later broadened his research to semi-supervised learning, co-authoring methods including FixMatch, ReMixMatch, and AdaMatch, and continues to work as a research scientist at Google.

profiles.hook: Anastasis Germanidis studied computer science at Wesleyan University before working as a backend engineer at Quantcast and Chartbeat. He then worked as a machine learning researcher in computer vision at IBM Research while completing a master's degree at NYU's Interactive Telecommunications Program. In 2018 he co-founded Runway with Cristóbal Valenzuela, building tools that brought machine learning models into creative video and image workflows for filmmakers and designers. As the company's research lead he helped drive its successive generative video models, including Gen-1, Gen-2, Gen-3 Alpha, and Gen-4, with Gen-3 Alpha named one of TIME's 100 Best Inventions of 2024. He has since expanded his role to Co-CEO alongside his continued work directing Runway's research.

profiles.hook: Andreas Blattmann carried out his early generative AI research in the CompVis group at LMU Munich, where he co-authored High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models in 2021, the paper that introduced the latent diffusion technique underlying Stable Diffusion. He went on to work as a researcher at NVIDIA and then at Stability AI, contributing to image and video generation systems that led to Stable Video Diffusion. In 2024 he co-founded Black Forest Labs alongside fellow former Stability AI and CompVis researchers Robin Rombach, Patrick Esser, and Dominik Lorenz, building the company from labs in Freiburg and San Francisco. Black Forest Labs released the FLUX family of text to image models, which quickly became a widely adopted open and commercial foundation for image generation, and Blattmann was named to Capital Magazin's Top 40 Under 40 in Germany in 2024.

profiles.hook: Andrej Karpathy has spent his career moving between building frontier neural networks and teaching other people how they work. He was a founding research scientist at OpenAI in 2015, then spent five years as Tesla's Director of AI leading the computer vision team behind Autopilot and Full Self-Driving. Along the way he designed and taught CS231n, Stanford's first deep learning course, and built a large public following through blog posts and YouTube lectures that walk through how language models are actually built. After a second stint at OpenAI and a run at his own AI education venture, Eureka Labs, he joined Anthropic's pretraining team in May 2026.

profiles.hook: Andrew Barto earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics and a PhD in computer and communication sciences, both from the University of Michigan. In 1977 he joined the University of Massachusetts Amherst as a postdoctoral research associate and spent his career there, rising through associate professor and professor to department chair before becoming Professor Emeritus of Information and Computer Sciences. Beginning in the 1980s, working closely with Richard Sutton, he developed the conceptual and algorithmic foundations of reinforcement learning, including temporal difference learning, policy gradient methods and agent designs that combine learning with planning. He and Sutton distilled that work into the textbook Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, first published in 1998 with a second edition in 2018, which became the standard reference for the field. In 2024 the Association for Computing Machinery awarded Barto and Sutton the ACM A.M. Turing Award for this body of work.

profiles.hook: Andrew Zisserman completed Part III of the Mathematical Tripos at Cambridge and a PhD in theoretical physics at Sunderland Polytechnic before moving into computer vision. He began vision research at the University of Edinburgh in 1984, and in 1987 joined Mike Brady's robotics group at the University of Oxford, where he worked on multiple view geometry and later founded the Visual Geometry Group. With Karen Simonyan he co-authored Very Deep Convolutional Networks for Large-Scale Image Recognition in 2014, introducing the VGGNet architecture that became a benchmark for deep convolutional networks in image recognition. He has been affiliated with Google DeepMind as a researcher since 2014, including work on the Flamingo visual language model, while continuing as a Royal Society Research Professor at Oxford.

profiles.hook: Antoine Bordes earned a PhD in artificial intelligence from Sorbonne University in Paris in 2010, work recognized with best doctoral research awards from the French Association for Artificial Intelligence and the French Armament Agency. He then held a postdoctoral position in Yoshua Bengio's lab at the University of Montreal and worked as a research scientist at CNRS in France. In 2013 he co-authored Translating Embeddings for Modeling Multi-relational Data, introducing TransE, a simple and influential method for embedding entities and relations from knowledge graphs into a shared vector space. He joined Facebook, later Meta, in 2014 and spent nine years building the Fundamental AI Research lab, serving as its global co-managing director for the final three years of his tenure. In March 2023 he left Meta to become Vice President of Artificial Intelligence at Helsing, a European defense technology company, where he leads AI research and engineering.

profiles.hook: Ashish Vaswani grew up partly in Oman before his family moved to Nagpur, India, when he was fifteen. He earned a bachelor's degree in computer science and engineering from Birla Institute of Technology, Mesra, worked briefly as a computer engineer in Delhi, then completed a master's degree and a PhD in computer science at the University of Southern California. He spent more than six years as a research scientist at Google Brain, and in 2017 he led the eight-author team, including Niki Parmar and Aidan Gomez, that published Attention Is All You Need, introducing the Transformer architecture that replaced recurrence and convolution with self-attention and became the base design for most later large language models. In April 2022 he co-founded Adept AI as chief scientist alongside Niki Parmar and David Luan, before leaving to co-found Essential AI with Parmar, where he now serves as CEO.

profiles.hook: Bernhard Schölkopf studied physics, mathematics and philosophy in Tübingen and London, then completed a doctorate in computer science at the Technical University of Berlin in 1997. He worked at the German National Research Center for Computer Science and held industrial research posts at AT&T Bell Laboratories, Microsoft Research and Biowulf Technologies, a period in which he helped develop the kernel methods that underlie the support vector machine framework used widely in machine learning. In 2001 he became a director and scientific member at the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics, and since 2011 he has directed the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems in Tübingen. His research has shifted toward causal machine learning, arguing that statistical learning methods need causal structure to generalize reliably outside their training distribution, work recognized with the 2019 Körber Prize. He also holds an honorary professorship at TU Berlin.

profiles.hook: Christian Szegedy was born in 1971 in Budapest, Hungary, and studied at Eotvos Lorand University before earning a PhD in mathematics from the University of Bonn. He worked in industry, including a stint at Cadence Design Systems, before joining Google around 2010, where he became part of the Google Brain team during the early years of the deep learning boom. In 2013 he co-authored the paper that first demonstrated adversarial examples in neural networks, showing that small, deliberate changes to an image could fool a classifier with high confidence. In 2014 he led the team that designed the Inception architecture, publicly known as GoogLeNet, which won the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge that year. The following year he and Sergey Ioffe introduced Batch Normalization, a training technique that became a near universal component of deep neural networks. He later moved from Google into work on frontier AI systems.

profiles.hook: Christopher Bishop earned a BA in physics from Oxford University and a PhD in theoretical physics, on quantum field theory, from the University of Edinburgh. He began his research career in fusion plasma physics at the Culham Laboratory, then moved into applied neural computing, heading the Applied Neurocomputing Centre at AEA Technology before taking a chair in the Department of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics at Aston University, where he founded and led the Neural Computing Research Group. He joined Microsoft Research in 1997 and later directed Microsoft Research Cambridge from 2015 to 2022. In 2022 he founded Microsoft Research AI4Science, which he continues to lead. He wrote the widely used textbooks Neural Networks for Pattern Recognition (1995) and Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (2006), and later co-authored Deep Learning: Foundations and Concepts (2024) with his son Hugh Bishop. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 2017.

profiles.hook: Christopher Manning grew up in Australia and earned a bachelor's degree with honors in mathematics, computer science, and linguistics from the Australian National University in 1989. He completed a PhD in linguistics at Stanford in 1994, then taught at Carnegie Mellon and the University of Sydney before returning to Stanford as a faculty member in 1999. Over the following two decades he built Stanford's Natural Language Processing Group into one of the most influential centers for language AI research in the world. In 2014 he and his students introduced GloVe, a widely used method for learning word vector representations from large text corpora. He went on to co-direct the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence and to hold the Thomas M. profiles.hook: David MacKay studied Natural Sciences at Trinity College, Cambridge, before completing a PhD at the California Institute of Technology in 1992 under John Hopfield, developing Bayesian methods for adaptive models. His 1992 paper 'A Practical Bayesian Framework for Backpropagation Networks' showed how Bayesian probability could be applied rigorously to neural networks, giving the field principled tools for model comparison and regularization. He returned to Cambridge, rising from Lecturer to Professor of Natural Philosophy in the Cavendish Laboratory, and in 2003 published Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms, a textbook that became a standard reference across machine learning and information theory and that he made freely available online. In 2009 he was appointed Chief Scientific Advisor to the UK Department of Energy and Climate Change, where he wrote the influential book Sustainable Energy Without the Hot Air, and in 2013 he became Cambridge's first Regius Professor of Engineering. MacKay was knighted in the 2016 New Year Honours for his services to scientific advice in government and science outreach, and he died of stomach cancer in April 2016 at the age of 48.

profiles.hook: David Rumelhart earned a bachelors degree in psychology and mathematics from the University of South Dakota before completing a PhD in mathematical psychology at Stanford University in 1967. He then joined the faculty at the University of California, San Diego, where he helped build the Parallel Distributed Processing research group that modeled cognition as patterns of activity distributed across networks of simple units. With Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams, he co-authored the 1986 Nature paper Learning Representations by Back Propagating Errors, which showed how multilayer neural networks could be trained efficiently and became one of the founding texts of modern deep learning. That same year he and James McClelland published the two volume Parallel Distributed Processing, Explorations in the Microstructure of Cognition, which brought connectionist ideas to a wide audience of psychologists, neuroscientists and computer scientists. He returned to Stanford as a professor in 1987, continuing his work in cognitive science until a neurodegenerative illness ended his research career in the late 1990s. He died in Chelsea, Michigan, on March 13, 2011, at the age of 68.

After running his own studio, Elixir Studios, he returned to academia and earned a PhD in cognitive neuroscience from University College London in 2009, studying memory and imagination. In 2010 he co-founded DeepMind with Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman to pursue general purpose learning systems, and Google acquired the company in 2014. Under his leadership DeepMind built landmark reinforcement learning systems, including AlphaGo, which defeated Go world champion Lee Sedol in 2016, and AlphaFold, which predicts the three dimensional structure of proteins from their amino acid sequences. Following a 2023 merger with Google Brain, he now leads the combined organization as co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind. In 2024 he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, shared with John Jumper and David Baker, for work on protein structure prediction, and was knighted for services to artificial intelligence.

In December 2015 he co-founded OpenAI, serving first as Research Director and later as Chief Scientist while the lab built its GPT model series. He left OpenAI in 2024 and co-founded Safe Superintelligence Inc with Daniel Gross and Daniel Levy, a company dedicated to a single goal, building safe superintelligence, and became its CEO in mid-2025 after Gross departed.

profiles.hook: Jascha Sohl-Dickstein worked across physics and neuroscience, including pre-doctoral work related to NASA Mars rover research, before turning fully to machine learning. He earned his PhD in 2012 at the Redwood Center for Theoretical Neuroscience at UC Berkeley, studying under Bruno Olshausen. He then worked as a research scientist and later principal scientist at Google Brain and Google DeepMind, studying the theory of large neural networks, learned optimizers, and the capabilities of large language models, before joining Anthropic as a member of technical staff.

profiles.hook: Jian Sun was born in Xi'an, China, in 1977 and earned his bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees, all from Xi'an Jiaotong University, completing his PhD in 2003. He then spent thirteen years at Microsoft Research Asia working on computer vision and computer graphics, contributing to technologies including Windows Hello facial recognition, Kinect Identity, and the Computer Vision and Face APIs for Microsoft Azure. The resulting ResNet architecture won the ImageNet and COCO competitions in 2015 and became one of the most widely used building blocks in computer vision. In July 2016 he joined Megvii, the Beijing based computer vision company behind Face++, as Chief Scientist and Managing Director of Research, and from January 2019 he also served as Dean of the College of Artificial Intelligence at Xi'an Jiaotong University. profiles.hook: Jimmy Ba completed his undergraduate degree at the University of Toronto in 2011 and his master's degree there in 2014, studying under Brendan Frey and Ruslan Salakhutdinov, before finishing his PhD under Geoffrey Hinton. He became an Assistant Professor in the Department of Computer Science at the University of Toronto, where he holds a CIFAR AI Chair and is affiliated with the Vector Institute. His research has continued to focus on efficient learning algorithms for deep neural networks, spanning reinforcement learning and natural language processing.

profiles.hook: Karen Spärck Jones studied history and moral sciences at Girton College, Cambridge, then turned to natural language processing and information retrieval, joining the Cambridge Language Research Unit and later the Computer Laboratory at the University of Cambridge. In 1972 she published A Statistical Interpretation of Term Specificity and Its Application in Retrieval, introducing inverse document frequency as a way to weight how informative a word is across a document collection. IDF became one half of TF-IDF, the weighting scheme that underpinned search engines for decades and remains a building block of modern text retrieval and vector search systems. She spent her career at Cambridge, served as president of the Association for Computational Linguistics, and was an outspoken advocate for women in computing.

He joined the Courant Institute at New York University in 2015, became a research scientist at Facebook AI Research from 2017 to 2020, and returned to lead work at NYU, later co-heading the Global AI Frontier Lab with Yann LeCun and taking a professorship in health statistics.

profiles.hook: Leo Breiman earned a physics degree from Caltech in 1949, a master's degree in mathematics from Columbia in 1950, and a PhD from UC Berkeley in 1954, after which he taught probability theory at UCLA. He later resigned his tenured position to spend more than a decade as an independent statistical consultant, working on problems like traffic pattern and ozone level prediction, before joining the UC Berkeley Department of Statistics faculty in 1980. With Jerome Friedman, Richard Olshen and Charles Stone he co-developed Classification and Regression Trees, published in 1984, and in 1996 he introduced Bagging, a method of averaging predictions across bootstrap samples to reduce variance. In 2001 he introduced Random Forests, an ensemble of randomized decision trees that became one of the most widely used machine learning algorithms, and published Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures, an influential essay on competing approaches to statistical inference. He died at his home in Berkeley, California, on July 5, 2005, following a prolonged illness.

profiles.hook: Llion Jones grew up in Wales and earned a master's degree in advanced computer science from the University of Birmingham. He joined Google in 2012, first working as a software engineer on YouTube before moving into machine intelligence and natural language research around 2015. In 2017 he was one of eight Google researchers who co-authored Attention Is All You Need, the paper that introduced the Transformer architecture now underlying most large language models. He spent nearly twelve years at Google, then left in August 2023, citing frustration with internal bureaucracy and difficulty getting access to compute and data. He co-founded Sakana AI in Tokyo that year with fellow ex-Google researcher David Ha, taking the role of Chief Technology Officer and pursuing nature-inspired approaches to AI research as an alternative to simply building ever larger models.

profiles.hook: Max Welling earned his PhD in 1998 at Utrecht University under Nobel laureate physicist Gerard t Hooft before moving into machine learning through postdoctoral positions at Caltech, University College London and the University of Toronto. In 2013 he and Diederik Kingma published Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes, introducing the variational autoencoder and a reparameterization trick that made it possible to train deep generative latent-variable models with backpropagation. He became a professor at the University of Amsterdam, where he directs the Amsterdam Machine Learning Lab, and in 2016 he and Thomas Kipf published Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks, extending convolutional architectures to graph-structured data. profiles.hook: Michael I. Jordan earned a master's degree in mathematics from Arizona State University and a PhD in cognitive science from the University of California, San Diego in 1985. He joined the faculty of MIT in 1988, before moving to the University of California, Berkeley in 1998. At Berkeley he holds the Pehong Chen Distinguished Professorship jointly in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences and the Department of Statistics. His research connects statistics, optimization and computer science, with major contributions to probabilistic graphical models, variational inference and Bayesian nonparametric methods that shaped how modern machine learning systems reason under uncertainty. He has also been an outspoken voice pushing back on hype around artificial general intelligence, arguing in his widely read 2018 essay that the field needs a genuine engineering discipline built around real world human centered systems rather than science fiction narratives about human imitative AI.

profiles.hook: Michael J. Jones earned his PhD from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1997. Working with Paul Viola, he co-developed the Viola-Jones object detection framework, published as Rapid Object Detection using a Boosted Cascade of Simple Features in 2001, which combined Haar-like features, an integral image representation and a cascade of boosted classifiers to make real-time face detection possible on ordinary hardware for the first time. The pair extended the work into Robust Real-Time Face Detection in 2004. Jones continued his career at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, where he became a Distinguished Research Scientist working on computer vision, machine learning and data analytics, including detection and analysis of people in images and video.

profiles.hook: Mustafa Suleyman was born in London in 1984 and studied at the University of Oxford. In 2010 he co-founded DeepMind, an artificial intelligence research lab that Google acquired in 2014, where he went on to lead applied AI and policy work. After leaving Google in 2019 and a period as a venture partner at Greylock, he co-founded Inflection AI in March 2022 with Reid Hoffman and Karen Simonyan, building the Pi personal assistant and the Inflection-2.5 model. In 2023 he published The Coming Wave, a book arguing that AI and synthetic biology pose a containment problem for governments and societies. In March 2024 he joined Microsoft as CEO of Microsoft AI, leading the Copilot consumer AI effort, and he has continued to write and speak about what he calls building humanist superintelligence.

profiles.hook: Niki Parmar earned a bachelor's degree in information technology from the Pune Institute of Computer Technology in India, then a master's degree in computer science from the University of Southern California. She joined Google in 2015 as an engineer and research scientist, working on end to end deep learning systems for natural language processing. In 2017, reportedly the youngest member of her team and the only one without a PhD, she co-authored Attention Is All You Need, the paper that introduced the Transformer architecture. She spent close to seven years at Google before co-founding Adept AI Labs in 2022 as Chief Technology Officer, building enterprise workflow automation tools, and then co-founding Essential AI in 2023 to build full stack AI products for automating data processing, with backing from Google and Nvidia. She has since also worked as a member of technical staff at Anthropic on reliable and interpretable AI systems.

profiles.hook: Noam Shazeer joined Google in 2000, where he first worked on improving the search engine's spelling correction and helped develop the PHIL algorithm that became central to Google AdSense. Over the next two decades he moved into deep learning, co-authoring a paper on sparsely gated mixture of experts models in 2016 and then, in 2017, co-authoring Attention Is All You Need, where he designed the multi-head attention mechanism at the core of the Transformer. He went on to create Mesh-TensorFlow in 2018 for training large Transformers across many machines, co-authored the T5 model in 2019, and contributed to Google's LaMDA dialogue system. In 2021 he left Google to co-found Character.AI with Daniel De Freitas, serving as its CEO and building one of the first consumer chatbots built on Transformer technology. In August 2024 he returned to Google as part of a licensing deal with Character.AI, rejoining Google DeepMind's research team, and later co-led development of the Gemini model as Vice President of Engineering before departing for OpenAI in June 2026.

profiles.hook: Oriol Vinyals was born in Sabadell, Spain, in 1983 and trained as both a mathematician and a telecommunications engineer at the Polytechnic University of Catalonia before completing graduate work at Carnegie Mellon and UC San Diego. He earned a PhD in electrical engineering and computer sciences from UC Berkeley in 2013, working on machine learning during internships at Google and Microsoft Research. He joined Google Brain the same year and helped develop sequence to sequence learning, a technique that let a single neural network translate and generate text without hand built rules. In 2016 he moved to Google DeepMind in London, where he became Vice President of Research and led the deep learning team behind AlphaStar, the system that beat professional StarCraft II players, and served as a technical co-lead on the Gemini model family. His sequence learning work also underpins AlphaFold, the protein structure system that won two of his DeepMind colleagues the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

profiles.hook: Patrick Esser studied computer vision at the IWR institute of Heidelberg University, working in Björn Ommer's Computer Vision group alongside Robin Rombach. In 2020 the pair co-authored VQGAN, published as Taming Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis, which combined a convolutional vector quantized autoencoder with a transformer to generate high resolution images. The following year he co-authored High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models with Rombach, Andreas Blattmann, Dominik Lorenz and Ommer, the paper that introduced latent diffusion and became the technical basis for Stable Diffusion. Esser and several of his CompVis colleagues later worked at Stability AI before leaving in 2024 to co-found Black Forest Labs with Rombach and Blattmann, an independent lab based in Freiburg, Germany, focused on generative visual models. The new company released its FLUX family of image generation models the same year it launched.

profiles.hook: Paul Viola was born in New York City on October 22, 1966, and studied at MIT, earning a PhD in 1995 with a thesis on alignment by maximization of mutual information under advisors Christopher Atkeson and Tomas Lozano-Perez. He went on to work at MIT, the Cambridge Research Laboratory of Compaq and Hewlett Packard, and Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories before joining Microsoft Research. In 2001, with Michael Jones, he published Rapid Object Detection using a Boosted Cascade of Simple Features, which combined Haar like features, an integral image representation and a cascade of boosted classifiers to detect faces in video in real time. The Viola-Jones framework became the standard method for real time face detection for more than a decade and was built into consumer cameras and photo software. Viola later held research and engineering leadership roles at Microsoft, Amazon Prime Air and the self driving vehicle company Zoox, continuing to work on computer vision and machine learning problems.

profiles.hook: Petar Veličković earned a Master of Arts with First Class Honours in Computer Science from the University of Cambridge in 2015, then stayed at Cambridge for a PhD in computer science at Trinity College, completed in 2019 under the supervision of Pietro Liò, with a thesis on the resurgence of structure in deep neural networks. During his doctorate he interned at Nokia Bell Labs and Jane Street and worked as a visiting researcher at the Mila Quebec AI Institute. In 2017 he led the team that introduced Graph Attention Networks, a neural architecture that lets nodes in a graph weigh the importance of their neighbors using self attention rather than fixed graph convolutions. He joined Google DeepMind in London in 2019, rising to Senior Staff Research Scientist, while remaining an Affiliated Lecturer at Cambridge, where he co-teaches a graduate course on geometric deep learning. His later work has applied graph neural networks to problems including travel time prediction in Google Maps and neural algorithmic reasoning, which studies how neural networks can learn to execute classical algorithms.

profiles.hook: Quoc Le was born in 1982 in Hương Thủy, in Vietnam's Thừa Thiên Huế province, and moved to Australia in 2004 to study at the Australian National University. He moved to the United States in 2007 for graduate study at Stanford University, where he earned a PhD in 2013 under Andrew Ng with a thesis on scalable feature learning. Le was a founding member of Google Brain in 2011, and in 2014 he co-authored the sequence to sequence learning paper with Ilya Sutskever and Oriol Vinyals, as well as an early version of the doc2vec method for learning vector representations of documents. In 2016 he began the AutoML project at Google Brain, which led to Neural Architecture Search with Reinforcement Learning, co-authored with Barret Zoph, showing that a neural network could design other neural networks that outperformed hand engineered ones. He later contributed to the Meena and LaMDA conversational models and to research on chain of thought prompting, and continues to work as a Distinguished Scientist at Google DeepMind.

profiles.hook: Richard Socher was born in 1983 in Dresden, Germany, and studied at the University of Leipzig and Saarland University before moving to Stanford University, where he earned a PhD in computer science in 2014 working on neural networks for natural language processing. In 2013 he co-authored Recursive Deep Models for Semantic Compositionality Over a Sentiment Treebank, which used recursive neural networks to parse the sentiment of entire sentences from their grammatical structure and introduced the widely used Stanford Sentiment Treebank dataset. In 2014, while finishing his doctorate, he founded the AI startup MetaMind, which Salesforce acquired in 2016, after which Socher served as the company's chief scientist and head of AI. In 2020 he co-founded You.com, an AI powered search engine, where he serves as CEO, and he later co-founded the venture firm AIX Ventures. Socher is widely credited with helping bring neural network methods into mainstream natural language processing research.

profiles.hook: Richard Sutton studied psychology at Stanford before moving into computer science at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, where he earned his PhD in 1984 working with Andrew Barto on the mathematical foundations of reinforcement learning. He went on to research positions in industry and academia before joining the University of Alberta, where he now holds the AITF Chair in Reinforcement Learning and Artificial Intelligence and serves as Chief Scientific Advisor to the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute. With Barto he wrote Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, the field's standard textbook, first published in 1998 and revised in 2018. He also holds a part-time research role at Google DeepMind and in 2022 helped found Keen Technologies with John Carmack to pursue artificial general intelligence. His 2019 essay The Bitter Lesson argued that general, computation-driven learning methods outperform approaches built on human-designed domain knowledge, a claim that shaped much of the field's later direction. In 2024 he and Barto received the ACM A.M. Turing Award for developing the conceptual and algorithmic foundations of reinforcement learning.

profiles.hook: Samy Bengio was born in Paris, France, in 1965 and studied computer science at the Université de Montréal, earning a PhD in 1993 with a thesis on optimizing parametric learning rules for neural networks. He spent the late 1990s and early 2000s at the IDIAP Research Institute and the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne in Switzerland before joining Google around 2008. At Google he became a leading research manager, helping build the Google Brain team and later leading a large machine learning research group that worked on sequence modeling, speech recognition and adversarial robustness. He left Google in 2021 to become senior director of AI and machine learning research at Apple, and in 2024 also took on an adjunct professorship at EPFL. Bengio has also served in leadership roles for the NeurIPS and ICLR conferences, including as NeurIPS program chair in 2017.

At Google he became one of the principal architects of the distributed systems that made the company's scale possible, co-designing the Google File System in 2003, MapReduce with Jeff Dean in 2004, Bigtable in 2006, and Spanner, Google's globally distributed database, in 2012. He has also contributed to Protocol Buffers, LevelDB, TensorFlow, and the Pathways distributed machine learning system. He now holds the title of Senior Fellow at Google, among the company's most senior technical positions, and has spent more than two decades building the infrastructure layer underneath Google's products and, later, its large-scale AI training systems.

profiles.hook: Sepp Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis at the Technical University of Munich diagnosed why deep and recurrent neural networks of the time failed to learn long-range dependencies, an analysis now known as the vanishing gradient problem. Working with his advisor Jurgen Schmidhuber, he developed Long Short-Term Memory networks as a solution, publishing the architecture in Neural Computation in 1997. LSTM became the dominant approach to sequence modeling for two decades, powering speech recognition and machine translation systems before the rise of Transformer models. After research positions at the University of Colorado Boulder and the Technical University of Berlin, Hochreiter joined Johannes Kepler University Linz, where he directed the Institute of Bioinformatics from 2006 and has led the Institute for Machine Learning since 2018. He also works on applying machine learning to genomics and other bioinformatics problems. In 2021 he received the IEEE Computational Intelligence Society Neural Networks Pioneer Award. He later founded NXAI, a Linz-based company building xLSTM, an extended memory architecture positioned as an alternative to Transformer models for sequence and time-series tasks.

profiles.hook: Sergey Ioffe earned his PhD in machine learning and computer vision from the University of California, Berkeley in 2001. He joined Google as a researcher in 2006 and spent the following years working on large scale image classification and deep network optimization. In 2015 he and Christian Szegedy published Batch Normalization, a technique that normalizes the inputs to each layer of a neural network during training. The method let researchers train much deeper networks with higher learning rates and far less careful weight initialization, and it was adopted almost immediately across the field. Ioffe continued this line of work with Batch Renormalization in 2017 and contributed to the Inception family of image recognition architectures. Ten years after its publication, the Batch Normalization paper received the ICML 2025 Test of Time Award.

profiles.hook: Shane Legg studied computer science at the University of Waikato and completed a master's degree at the University of Auckland before pursuing doctoral research at the Dalle Molle Institute for Artificial Intelligence Research (IDSIA) under Marcus Hutter. His PhD thesis, Machine Super Intelligence, set out an early formal research agenda for artificial general intelligence, and with Hutter he proposed a mathematical definition of machine intelligence that became a reference point for later work on measuring progress toward general AI. In 2010 he co-founded DeepMind Technologies with Demis Hassabis and Mustafa Suleyman, a company Google acquired in 2014. He has written publicly, including on his personal blog, about probabilistic forecasts for when machine intelligence might reach human levels. He was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 2019 for services to artificial intelligence. When DeepMind and Google's Brain team merged in April 2023 to form Google DeepMind, Legg remained part of the unit's core leadership group and continued his research role focused on artificial general intelligence.

profiles.hook: Terry Sejnowski earned a BS in physics from Case Western Reserve University and a PhD in physics from Princeton University, followed by postdoctoral work in biology at Princeton and in neurobiology at Harvard Medical School. In 1985 he co-authored A Learning Algorithm for Boltzmann Machines with David Ackley and Geoffrey Hinton, introducing a stochastic learning method for neural networks. Working with Charles Rosenberg, he then built NETtalk, a neural network that learned to convert written English text into speech sounds, published in 1987 in Complex Systems and widely cited as an early demonstration that distributed neural networks could learn a complex cognitive task from examples. In 1988 he moved to the Salk Institute for Biological Studies, where he now holds the Francis Crick Chair and directs the Computational Neurobiology Laboratory, with a joint appointment at the University of California, San Diego. He founded the journal Neural Computation in 1989 and has served as its editor-in-chief since, and in 2018 he co-authored the book The Deep Learning Revolution. He was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 2010 and has since received the Gruber Neuroscience Prize and the Brain Prize.

profiles.hook: Thomas Cover was born in San Bernardino, California, in 1938. He earned a BS in physics from MIT in 1960 and then moved to Stanford, completing an MS in 1961 and a PhD in electrical engineering in 1964. He joined the Stanford faculty the same year and remained there for the rest of his career, holding a joint appointment in electrical engineering and statistics. In 1967 he and Peter Hart published Nearest Neighbor Pattern Classification, proving that a simple rule of comparing a new example to its closest labeled neighbors could not do much worse than the best possible classifier, a result that became a founding theorem of pattern recognition. He went on to make major contributions to broadcast channel coding and portfolio theory, and in 1991 he and Joy Thomas published Elements of Information Theory, which became the standard graduate textbook in the field. He died at Stanford Hospital on March 26, 2012, at age 73.

He completed his PhD cum laude in 2020 and joined Google Brain in Amsterdam as a research scientist that same year. He has since worked on relational reasoning, world models, and object-centric learning, and holds the title of Senior Staff Research Scientist at Google DeepMind.

profiles.hook: Tianqi Chen built his reputation as a graduate student by creating tools that made machine learning systems faster and easier to deploy at scale. He earned bachelor's and master's degrees from Shanghai Jiao Tong University before completing a PhD at the University of Washington's Paul G. Allen School in 2019, advised by Carlos Guestrin. During his PhD he created XGBoost, a gradient boosting library that became a default choice for structured data problems in industry and machine learning competitions, and he co-created Apache MXNet, an early deep learning framework, and Apache TVM, a compiler that lets deep learning models run efficiently across many kinds of hardware. In 2019 he co-founded OctoML, later renamed OctoAI, serving as its chief technologist to commercialize the machine learning compilation techniques behind TVM, and the company was acquired by NVIDIA in 2024. He is now an Associate Professor in the Machine Learning and Computer Science Departments at Carnegie Mellon University and a Distinguished Engineer at NVIDIA, and he continues to lead open source projects including MLC-LLM for deploying large language models on everyday devices.

profiles.hook: Tom Mitchell helped establish machine learning as an academic discipline in its own right. He earned a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from MIT in 1973 and a PhD from Stanford University in 1979, studying under Bruce Buchanan. After teaching at Rutgers University, he joined Carnegie Mellon University in 1986, where he became the E. Fredkin Professor and later the founding chair of the world's first Machine Learning Department in 2006. In 1997 he published the textbook Machine Learning, one of the first comprehensive textbooks in the field and still used in university courses. His later research pushed machine learning into new territory, including the Never-Ending Language Learner project, which continuously extracts facts from web text, and work using brain imaging to study how the brain represents word meaning. He has also studied the effects of AI on the labor market, co-chairing a National Academies report on AI and the future of work.

profiles.hook: Tomas Mikolov began experimenting with neural language models as a student in the Czech Republic in 2007, work that fed into his PhD at Brno University of Technology, completed in 2012, on recurrent neural network models of language. He joined Google as a research scientist and in 2013 published Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space with Kai Chen, Greg Corrado, and Jeffrey Dean, introducing the word2vec algorithm for learning dense vector representations of words from raw text. The technique made semantic relationships between words computable through simple vector arithmetic and was adopted across natural language processing almost overnight. Later that year he co-authored Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality, which introduced negative sampling and extended the method to phrases. He moved to Facebook AI Research in 2014, where he later contributed to the fastText library for efficient text classification and word representation across more than 150 languages. In 2019 he was named a Neuron Award laureate, and he has since led a research group at the CIIRC institute of the Czech Technical University in Prague.

profiles.hook: Vladimir Vapnik developed much of the mathematical foundation that modern machine learning still relies on. Born in Tashkent in the Soviet Union, he earned his doctorate in statistics from the Institute of Control Sciences in Moscow in 1964, where he later headed the computer science research department. Working with Alexey Chervonenkis, he developed what became known as Vapnik-Chervonenkis theory, a mathematical framework for understanding when and why a learning algorithm can generalize from training data to new examples. After moving to the United States, he joined AT&T Bell Labs, where he and colleagues including Corinna Cortes, Bernard Boser, and Isabelle Guyon turned his theoretical work into the support vector machine, a classification method described in a landmark 1995 paper with Cortes and in a US patent he shares with Boser and Guyon. He went on to hold research and teaching positions at NEC Laboratories, Royal Holloway University of London, Columbia University, and Facebook AI Research, continuing to develop and extend statistical learning theory.

profiles.hook: Xiangyu Zhang enrolled at Xi'an Jiaotong University in 2008 and completed a bachelor's degree in software engineering in 2012. He then entered a joint PhD program between Xi'an Jiaotong University and Microsoft Research Asia, working under Jian Sun and Kaiming He. As part of that team he co-authored Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition in 2015, contributing the underlying framework and implementation for what became known as ResNet, a network design that let researchers train models hundreds of layers deep. He later worked as a Principal Researcher at Megvii, where in 2017 and 2018 he led the development of ShuffleNet, a convolutional architecture designed specifically to run efficiently on mobile devices with limited computing power. According to industry reporting, he subsequently joined the Chinese large language model company StepFun as Chief Scientist.

profiles.hook: Yang Song earned a BS in mathematics and physics from Tsinghua University in 2016, graduating magna cum laude, and then began a PhD in computer science at Stanford University advised by Stefano Ermon. In 2019 he published Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution, which proposed learning the gradient of a data distribution's log density, called its score function, and using it to generate samples through a Langevin-style sampling process. In 2021 he extended this idea with Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations, unifying score-based models and diffusion models into a single continuous-time framework and winning an ICLR Outstanding Paper Award. After completing his PhD in 2022 he joined OpenAI, where he led a strategic explorations team and co-authored Consistency Models, a method for generating samples in a single step without adversarial training. In 2025 he joined Meta Superintelligence Labs as a Research Principal.

profiles.hook: Yann LeCun helped build the technique that underlies most of today's computer vision systems. He earned a PhD in computer science from Universite Pierre et Marie Curie in Paris in 1987, working on early ideas that fed into backpropagation based neural network training. At AT&T Bell Labs starting in 1988, he developed convolutional neural networks and built LeNet, a system for reading handwritten digits that was later deployed commercially to process a large share of checks handled by US banks. He went on to become a professor at New York University's Courant Institute, founding the NYU Center for Data Science, and in 2013 joined Facebook, later Meta, as founding director and then Chief AI Scientist of its AI research division. In 2018 he shared the ACM A.M. Turing Award with Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio for their work on deep learning. He left Meta in November 2025 after roughly twelve years to launch Advanced Machine Intelligence Labs, a venture focused on building AI systems around world models rather than only predicting text.

profiles.hook: Yoshua Bengio has spent his career pushing neural networks from a marginal idea into the foundation of modern AI, and more recently has turned much of his attention to the risks that AI now poses. Born in Paris and raised in Canada, he earned a PhD in computer science from McGill University before joining the Universite de Montreal, where he has been a professor since the early 1990s. His 2003 paper A Neural Probabilistic Language Model helped establish the use of learned word representations in language modeling, an idea that became central to later large language models, and in 2014 he co-authored the paper introducing generative adversarial networks with Ian Goodfellow and others. He founded Mila, the Quebec Artificial Intelligence Institute, building it into one of the world's largest academic centers for deep learning research, and in 2016 co-founded the AI startup Element AI. In 2018 he shared the ACM A.M. Turing Award with Yann LeCun and Geoffrey Hinton for his contributions to deep learning. In recent years he has chaired the International AI Safety Report and, in June 2025, launched LawZero, a nonprofit research organization focused on building safe, non-agentic AI systems.
